'''Ned D. Heindel''' (September 4, 1937 – June 27, 2023) was an American chemist. He was the Howard S. Bunn Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at [[Lehigh University]], where he continued to do research.<ref name="Emeritus"/> Heindel also worked as a medical research consultant.<ref name="Finn">{{cite web|last1=Finn|first1=John|title=Helen Murray Free Lectures Feature Pharmaceutical Expert|url=https://www.wooster.edu/news/releases/2015/october/lecture-murrayfree/|website=Wooster|date=1 October 2015|access-date=10 October 2017|archive-date=4 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171204171147/https://www.wooster.edu/news/releases/2015/october/lecture-murrayfree/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Bowker"/><ref name="Bloomberg">{{cite web|title=Ned Heindel Ph.D.|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/research/stocks/private/person.asp?personId=116696083&privcapId=28397097&previousCapId=30995038&previousTitle=20/20%20HealthCare%20Partners%20LLC|website=Bloomberg|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> Heindel's research focused on diagnostic and therapeutic drug development. He served as [[Presidents of the American Chemical Society|president of the American Chemical Society]] in 1994,<ref name="Carpenter">{{cite journal|last1=Carpenter|first1=Ernest|title=Ned Heindel chosen ACS president-elect|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=23 November 1992|volume=70|issue=47|pages=5–6|doi=10.1021/cen-v070n047.p005a}}</ref> and has twice chaired the ACS Division for the History of Chemistry.<ref name="LehighBio"/> 

== Early life ==
Ned Duane Heindel was born on September 4, 1937, in  [[Red Lion, York County, Pennsylvania]], to Mr. and Mrs. Penrose H. Heindel.<ref name="LehighBio"/><ref name="Bunn"/><ref name="Bowker"/> He earned a B.S. in chemistry from [[Lebanon Valley College]] (1959), and a master's degree (1961) and Ph.D. (1963) from the [[University of Delaware]],<ref name="Kaufman">{{cite news|last1=Kaufman|first1=Ron|title=People: Lehigh Professor Is Named Chemical Society's President-Elect|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/16909/title/People--Lehigh-Professor-Is-Named-Chemical-Society-s-President-Elect/|accessdate=10 October 2017|work=The Scientist|date=January 11, 1993}}</ref> 
where he worked with William A. Mosher.<ref name="Emeritus"/>
He did postdoctoral work at [[Princeton University]] in 1964<ref name="Safety">{{cite book|last1=Committee on Promoting Safe and Secure Chemical Management in Developing Countries, Board on Chemical Sciences and Technology, Division on Earth and Life Studies, National Research Council of the National Academies|title=Promoting chemical laboratory safety and security in developing countries|date=2010|publisher=National Academies Press|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=978-0309150415|pages=75|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4KYzOUrr9lsC&pg=PT91|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> with [[Edward C. Taylor]].<ref name="Emeritus"/>

== Career ==
After teaching briefly at [[Ohio University]] and [[Marshall University]] Heindel joined the faculty at [[Lehigh University]] in 1966. He became a full professor by 1973,<ref name="Emeritus"/> and was named the Howard S. Bunn Distinguished Professor of Organic Chemistry in 1976.<ref name="Bowker">{{cite book|title=American Men & Women of Science, 1995-96: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological and Related Sciences|date=1996|publisher=R. R. Bowker|location=New Providence, New Jersey|isbn=978-0835234665|volume=3|pages=739–740|edition=19th}}</ref><ref name="Henderson">{{cite book |editor-last1=Henderson |editor-first1=Andrea Kovacs |chapter=Heindel, Ned Duane |title=American Men & Women of Science: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences |date=2010 |publisher=Gale|volume=3 |location=Detroit |page=701 |edition=28th |chapter-url=http://link.galegroup.com/apps/doc/CX2469848565/GVRL?u=othmerloc&sid=GVRL&xid=2711e7b2 |accessdate=11 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="Bunn">{{cite news|title=Awarded Chemistry Recognition Dr. Ned D. Heindel Red Lion|url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/81585658/|accessdate=10 October 2017|work=York Daily Record from York, Pennsylvania|page=6|date=June 2, 1976}}</ref>

Heindel also served as a visiting professor of radiation oncology at [[Hahnemann University Hospital]] from 1971 to 2006, and as director of the Center for Health Sciences at Lehigh University from 1980 to 1987. He helped to establish the Lehigh-Hahnemann Cooperative Medical Education Program from 1992 to 2017 and was involved in Lehigh's distance education program.<ref name="Emeritus"/>

He became professor emeritus in 2018. He continues to do research (e.g. healing burn wounds<ref>{{cite web |title=Newsletter of the Lehigh Valley Section |date=October 2018 |volume=101 |number=7 |page=2 |url=https://lvacs.sites.acs.org/Octagons/October2018.pdf |website=American Chemical Society, Lehigh Valley Section |accessdate=5 October 2018 |archive-date=6 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181006000907/https://lvacs.sites.acs.org/Octagons/October2018.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>) and works as a medical research consultant.<ref name="Emeritus">{{cite news |title= Transitioning into a renewed focus on excellence |url= https://chemistry.cas2.lehigh.edu/sites/chemistry.cas2.lehigh.edu/files/doc-newsletter-f18-no48-9-25-18-min.pdf |accessdate= 5 October 2018 |pages= 4–5, 18 |work= MUDD in your eye |agency= Lehigh University, Department of Chemistry |issue= Fall |date= 2018 |archive-date= 6 October 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181006000829/https://chemistry.cas2.lehigh.edu/sites/chemistry.cas2.lehigh.edu/files/doc-newsletter-f18-no48-9-25-18-min.pdf |url-status= dead }}</ref>

===Science===
Heindel's research focuses on diagnostic and therapeutic drug development, including the areas of [[cancer]] research, [[nuclear medicine]], diagnostic [[Radiopharmacology|radioactive pharmaceuticals]],<ref name="Bowker"/><ref>{{cite book |editor-last1=Heindel |editor-first1=Ned D. |title=The Chemistry of radiopharmaceuticals |date=1978 |publisher=Masson Pub. USA |location=New York |isbn=978-0893520199}}</ref><ref name="Welch">{{cite book |last1=Welch |first1=Michael J. |title=Radiopharmaceuticals and Other Compounds Labelled with Short-Lived Radionuclides |date=September 24, 2013 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-1483104164 |page=77 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TvD8BAAAQBAJ&q=Heindel+radiopharmaceuticals&pg=PA77 |accessdate=12 June 2018}}</ref> [[chemotherapeutics]] and tumor-associated [[monoclonal antibodies]].<ref name="CounterACT">{{cite web|title=Ned D. Heindel, Ph.D.|url=http://counteract.rutgers.edu/faculty/heindel.html|website=UMDNJ-Rutgers University CounterACT Research Center of Excellence|accessdate=10 October 2017|archive-date=15 May 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150515103030/http://counteract.rutgers.edu/faculty/heindel.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> He has applied for at least 20 patents, with 14 issued.<ref name="Emeritus"/><ref name="Safety"/><ref name="Justia">{{cite web|title=Patents by Inventor Ned D. Heindel|url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/ned-d-heindel|website=Justia Patents|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> 
He has published more than 260 papers.<ref name="Emeritus"/><ref>{{cite web|title=Ned D. Heindel|url=https://chemistry.cas2.lehigh.edu/faculty/ned-d-heindel|website=Lehigh University|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> A number of candidate pharmaceuticals from his lab have reached advanced animal trials.<ref name="Salter">{{cite news |last1=Salter |first1=Rosa |title=Lehigh Professor's Patent Pays Off For Blood Sterilization |url=https://www.mcall.com/1995/08/28/lehigh-professors-patent-pays-off-for-blood-sterilization/ |access-date=11 June 2018 |work=The Morning Call |date=August 28, 1995}}</ref><ref name="Joseph"/>

He proved that [[psoralens]] and [[coumarins]] can be useful as photoactivated inhibitors of [[epidermal growth factor]].<ref name="Bourke, Jr.">{{cite web |last1=Bourke  |first1=Frederic A. Jr.|title=US20140341845A1: Methods and systems for treating cell proliferation related disorders |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US20140341845 |website=US Patents |accessdate=11 June 2018|quote="U.S. Pat. No. 5,216,176 of Heindel discloses a large number of psoralens and coumarins that have some effectiveness as photoactivated inhibitors of epidermal growth factor. Halogens and amines are included among the vast functionalities that could be included in the psoralen/coumarin backbone."}}</ref><ref name="Acton">{{cite book |last1=Acton |first1=Q. Ashton |title=Advances in DNA Research and Application |date=June 21, 2013 |publisher=Scholarly Editions |location=Atlanta, Georgia |isbn=978-1481682350 |page=169 |edition=2013 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=F57riHYkx74C&pg=PA169 |accessdate=11 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="Choudhuri">{{cite journal |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |last2=Choudhuri |first2=Mridula |last3=Ressner |first3=Joel |last4=Foster |first4=Natalie |title=Aminomethyl psoralens. Electrophilic substitution of hydroxymethylphthalimide on linear furocoumarins |journal=Journal of Heterocyclic Chemistry |date=January 1985 |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=73–76 |doi=10.1002/jhet.5570220119 }}</ref><ref name="Van Dongen">{{cite journal |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |last2=Van Dongen |first2=Jacobus M.A.M. |last3=Sachais |first3=Bruce S. |last4=Phillips |first4=John H. |last5=Gallo |first5=Michael A. |last6=Laskin |first6=Jeffrey D. |title=Syntheses of Psoralen Analogues and Evaluation of Their Inhibition of Epidermal Growth Factor Binding |journal=Journal of Pharmaceutical Sciences |date=July 1991 |volume=80 |issue=7 |pages=686–689 |doi=10.1002/jps.2600800715 |pmid=1941569 |url=https://jpharmsci.org/article/S0022-3549(15)48584-3/pdf |accessdate=11 June 2018|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
[[Photosensitizers]] are used to treat epidermal proliferation, [[psoriasis]] and [[vitiligo]]. 
Heindel's lab has identified a new structural family of organic molecules which perform as light-activated anti-cancer compounds. After activation by [[ultraviolet light]], lipophilic dipyranone (NDH2476) was found to inhibit abnormal [[Keratinocyte]] growth with an IC50 of 9 nanomolar concentration. NDH2476 acts through initial [[Intercalation (biochemistry)|intercalation into DNA]] and when irradiated, “nicks” the [[polynucleotide]] and prevents subsequent unwinding. Gem di-methylation, double bond [[hydrogenation]], or non-linear, angular geometry to the dipyranone greatly reduced or even eliminated the photo-cytotoxicity.<ref name="Laskin">{{cite journal |last1=Laskin |first1=Jeffrey D. |last2=Jan |first2=Yi-Hua |last3=Jetter |first3=Michele M. |last4=Guillon |first4=Christophe D. |last5=Mariano |first5=Thomas M. |last6=Heck |first6=Diane E. |last7=Heindel |first7=Ned D. |title=Identification of a Pyranocoumarin Photosensitizer that is a Potent Inhibitor of Keratinocyte Growth |journal=Photochemistry and Photobiology |date=May 2018 |volume=94 |issue=3 |pages=577–582 |doi=10.1111/php.12882 |pmid=29315592 |s2cid=3634344 }}</ref>

Heindel was one of the principal investigators in Project CounterACT-Rutgers, studying antidotes to [[sulfur mustard]] gas poisoning.<ref name="Lally">{{cite news|last1=Lally|first1=Robin|title=Rutgers Receives $19 Million to Develop Drugs to Treat Chemical Weapons Attacks Work aimed at devising drug therapies to counteract deadly chemical poisons|url=https://news.rutgers.edu/news/rutgers-receives-19-million-develop-drugs-treat-chemical-weapons-attacks/20161130|accessdate=10 October 2017|work=Rutgers Today|date=December 1, 2016}}</ref><ref name="Safety"/> 
Heindel's lab has developed an [[indomethacin]] [[prodrug]], NDH4338, designed for use as a wound-healing accelerant for [[vesicant]]-triggered [[skin lesions]]. The drug is a trifunctional pharmaceutical composed of covalently linked inhibitors of [[COX-2]], [[acetylcholinesterase]], and induced [[nitric oxide synthase]] which can be released [[in vivo]] from the parent molecule. It has been tested on rodents pre-exposed to chloroethyl ethyl sulfide, [[nitrogen mustard]], and sulfur mustard and has shown a marked acceleration of wound healing. While NDH4338 has several mechanisms of action, a principle one is suppression of [[mast cell]] [[degranulation]] in skin.<ref name="Joseph">{{cite journal |last1=Joseph |first1=Laurie B. |last2=Composto |first2=Gabriella M. |last3=Perez |first3=Roberto M. |last4=Kim |first4=Hong-Duck |last5=Casillas |first5=Robert P. |last6=Heindel |first6=Ned D. |last7=Young |first7=Sherri C. |last8=Lacey |first8=Carl J. |last9=Saxena |first9=Jaya |last10=Guillon |first10=Christophe D. |last11=Croutch |first11=Claire R. |last12=Laskin |first12=Jeffrey D. |last13=Heck |first13=Diane E. |title=Sulfur mustard induced mast cell degranulation in mouse skin is inhibited by a novel anti-inflammatory and anticholinergic bifunctional prodrug |journal=Toxicology Letters |date=September 2018 |volume=293 |pages=77–81 |doi=10.1016/j.toxlet.2017.11.005 |pmid=29127031 |pmc=5938161 }}</ref><ref name="Lacey">{{cite journal |last1=Lacey |first1=Carl J. |last2=Wohlman |first2=Irene |last3=Guillon |first3=Christophe |last4=Saxena |first4=Jaya |last5=Fianu-Velgus |first5=Cynthia |last6=Aponte |first6=Erik |last7=Young |first7=Sherri C. |last8=Heck |first8=Diane E. |last9=Joseph |first9=Laurie B. |last10=Laskin |first10=Jeffrey D. |last11=Heindel |first11=Ned D. |title=Multi-inhibitor prodrug constructs for simultaneous delivery of anti-inflammatory agents to mustard-induced skin injury |journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences |date=August 2016 |volume=1378 |issue=1 |pages=174–179 |doi=10.1111/nyas.13177 |pmid=27505078 |pmc=5063683 |bibcode=2016NYASA1378..174L }}</ref>

[[Hydroxamate]] compounds developed by Heindel's lab have been found to enhance [[corneal]] wound healing after mustard exposure.  Compounds studied include olvanil OH (NDH4409) and retro olvanil 8 (NDH4417). Hydroxamates reduced the activity of [[ADAM17]] and [[matrix metalloproteinases]] (MMPs), and attenuated expression of [[EMMPRIN]], a tumor cell surface inducer of MMPs. This resulted in less epithelial sloughing, improved protection of the [[basement membrane zone]], and better epithelial-stromal integrity after injury.<ref name="Gordon">{{cite journal |last1=Gordon |first1=Marion |last2=Rodrigues |first2=Andrea |last3=Hahn |first3=Rita |last4=Gerecke |first4=Donald |author5-link=Kathy Svoboda |last5=Svoboda |first5=Kathy |last6=Heindel |first6=Ned |title=Corneal Wound Healing is Facilitated by Hydroxamates that Reduce EMMPRIN Expression |journal=Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science |date=June 2013 |volume=54 |page=3910 |url=http://iovs.arvojournals.org/article.aspx?articleid=2148730 |accessdate=12 June 2018}}</ref>

He served on the board of directors of the Pennsylvania Drug Discovery Institute,<ref name="PDDI">{{cite web|title=Board of Directors|url=http://www.padrugdiscovery.org/aboutus/boardofdirectors.html|website=Pennsylvania Drug Discovery Institute|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> and the Scientific Advisory Board of Azevan Pharmaceuticals, Inc.<ref name="Bloomberg"/>

Heindel held a number of positions in the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS), since first becoming a board member in 1985.<ref name="Carpenter"/>
In 1994, Heindel served as President of the ACS.<ref name="BD">{{cite web|title=ACS Presidents, A Chronological List|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/about/president/acspresidents.html|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref><ref name="Wilson">{{cite journal|last1=Wilson|first1=Elizabeth|title=Luminaries highlight chemistry's contributions|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=8 February 1999|volume=77|issue=6|pages=38|doi=10.1021/cen-v077n006.p038a}}</ref>
In 2009 Heindel was named an ACS Fellow.<ref name="Fellow">{{cite web|title=ACS Fellows|url=https://www.acs.org/content/dam/acsorg/funding/fellows/acs-fellows-list.xlsx|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref>

===History===
Heindel served on the board of directors of the National Foundation for History of Chemistry,<ref name="Achilladelis">{{cite book|last1=Achilladelis|first1=Basil|last2=Bowden|first2=Mary Ellen|title=Structures of Life: To Accompany an Exhibit by the Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry|date=1989|publisher=Beckman Center for the History of Chemistry|location=Philadelphia, Pa.|isbn=978-0-941901-07-9|page=37|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DhlU3sJYb_8C&pg=PA37|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref>
and has twice been chairperson of the ACS Division of the History of Chemistry.<ref name="LehighBio">{{cite web|title=Biography: Ned Heindel|url=http://nheindel.cas2.lehigh.edu/content/biography|website=Lehigh University|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref>
Heindel has been credited with chairing a task force formed by the ACS in 1979 to consider the creation of a national center for the history of chemistry,<ref name=HistoryCHF/> but he himself credits [[John H. Wotiz]] with that chairmanship.<ref name="Magazine">{{cite journal |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned  |title= The story behind the story |journal= Chemical Heritage Magazine |publisher= [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] |date=2000|volume=18 |issue=3 |page=45 }}</ref> In December 1981 the ACS approved the establishment of the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation|Center for the History of Chemistry]] in Philadelphia.<ref name=HistoryCHF>{{cite journal|title=The History of CHF|journal=Chemical Heritage: Newsmagazine of the Chemical Heritage Foundation|date=2000-02-01|volume=18|issue=1|pages=16–22}}</ref><ref name=CHOC18-3>{{cite journal|last=Wotiz|first=John H.|title=History of Chemistry: The ACS Centre in Philadelphia |journal=Chemical Heritage|date=2000|volume=18|issue=3|pages=45–46}}</ref> He was a contributor to a [[Nova (American TV series)|NOVA]] program about [[Percy Julian]], “Forgotten Genius”, which aired in 2007.<ref name="Emeritus"/>

He wrote both papers and books relating history and chemistry. Among his publications he has examined "The Professionalization of American Chemistry: How the German Ph.D. Model Crossed the Atlantic",<ref name="Rasmussen">{{cite book |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |last2=Sturchio |first2=Jeffrey L. |last3=Bohning |first3=James J. |editor-last=Rasmussen |editor-first=Seth C. |title=Igniting the Chemical Ring of Fire |date=2018 |publisher=World Scientific |location=New Jersey |isbn=978-1-78634-454-0 |pages=387–426|chapter=Chapter 14: The Professionalization of American Chemistry: How the German Ph.D. Model Crossed the Atlantic |doi=10.1142/9781786344557_0014 }}</ref>
and the careers of early [[photochemistry|photochemists]] such as [[Giacomo Ciamician]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |last2=Pfau |first2=Michel A. |title=A profitable partnership: Giacomo Ciamician and Paul Silber |journal=Journal of Chemical Education |date=July 1965 |volume=42 |issue=7 |pages=383 |doi=10.1021/ed042p383|bibcode=1965JChEd..42..383H }}</ref>

Another area of interest is the medicinal chemistry and folk-healing techniques of the [[Pennsylvania Dutch]].
''The Nineteenth Century Horse Doctor: A Pennsylvania Dutchman's Practical Guide to Treating Horses'' recognized the essential role of the horse in pre-industrial North American farming. Heindel and Robert D. Rapp translate and examine recipes in 19th century books of veterinary practice, or "Pferdartz", from the Moravian and the Pennsylvania Dutch traditions. Folk medicine cures ranged from herbs, minerals, poultices, and bleeding to incantations.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Nineteenth Century Horse Doctor: A Pennsylvania Dutchman's Practical Guide to Treating Horses |url=http://coffeetownpress.com/the-nineteenth-century-horse-doctor-a-pennsylvania-dutchmans-practical-guide-to-treating-horses/ |website=Coffeetown Press |date=8 August 2011 |accessdate=11 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="Rapp">{{cite book |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |last2=Rapp |first2=Robert D. |title=The Nineteenth-century horse doctor : a Pennsylvania Dutchman's practical guide for treating horses |date=2011 |publisher=Coffeetown Press |location=Seattle, WA |isbn=9781603811217}}</ref>

In ''Hexenkopf, History, Healing and Hexerei'', he examines traditions of both white and black magic in the Wilhelm and Saylor families of [[Northampton County, Pennsylvania]]. Healers such as [[Johann Peter Seilor]]<ref name="White">{{cite book |last1=White |first1=Thomas |title=Witches of Pennsylvania : occult history & lore |date=2013 |publisher=Arcadia Publishing |isbn=978-1626191327 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=riiACQAAQBAJ&pg=PT39}}</ref> and [[Emanuel Wilhelm]] used tonics, personalized prescriptions and manipulations to treat sickness and fight off evil in the tradition of white magic or "[[Braucherei]]". Modern pharmaceutical science has examined the use of some of their treatments such as [[poke root]] and [[mayapple]] root.<ref name="Bentley">{{cite news |last1=Bentley |first1=Tiffany |title=Witchcraft in Williams Township, a history of the good and evil |url=http://www.lehighvalleylive.com/events/index.ssf/2011/10/witchcraft_in_williams_townshi.html |accessdate=11 June 2018 |work=Lehigh Valley Live |date=Oct 29, 2011}}</ref> Traditions of black magic have focused on [[Hexenkopf Hill|Hexenkopf Rock]].<ref name="Merlin">{{cite news |last1=Merlin |first1=Michelle |title=Haunted rock legends live on in technology, religion |url=https://www.apnews.com/079df2401a384304a5eaebefbf30ebaa |accessdate=11 June 2018 |work=AP |date=October 30, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Heindel |first1=Ned D. |title=Hexenkopf: History, Healing and Hexerei |date=2009 |publisher=Northampton County Historical and Genealogical Society |isbn=978-1877701177 |edition=2nd}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=On the Shelf: Hexenkopf: History, Healing and Hexerei |url=https://danharms.wordpress.com/2006/08/07/on-the-shelf-hexenkopf-history-healing-and-hexerei/ |website=Papers Falling from an Attic Window |accessdate=11 June 2018|date=2006-08-06 }}</ref>

Heindel and his wife Linda (Heefner) Heindel were active in historical groups in the [[Lehigh Valley]]<ref name="Folklife">{{cite journal|title=Contributors|url=http://digitalcommons.ursinus.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1134&context=pafolklifemag|accessdate=10 October 2017|journal=Pennsylvania Folklife Magazine|volume=41|issue=3|date=1992}}</ref> and frequently contribute to ''Pennsylvania Folklife Magazine''.<ref name="Ursinus">{{cite web|title=Pennsylvania Folklife Magazine|url=http://digitalcommons.ursinus.edu/pafolklifemag/index.2.html|website=Digital Commons at Ursinus|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref> 
Heindel has lectured on social relationships between Europeans, [[Lenni Lenape]], and [[Shawnee]] in the [[Durham, Pennsylvania|Durham area]] in the 1700s. He is  interested in the work of the Buckwampum Historical and Literary Society,<ref name="Sigafoos">{{cite book|title=Bucks County Historical Society Papers|last=Sigafoos|first=Lewis|publisher=Bucks Country Historical Society|year=1935|editor-last=Fackenthal|editor-first=B.F.|volume=7|pages=414–419|language=en|chapter=Buckwampum Historical and Literary Society|chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/buckscountyhisto07buck#page/414/mode/2up}}</ref> a group that met from 1888 to 1903. Most were amateurs but archaeologist [[Henry Mercer]] was also a member. The group conducted several digs in [[Bucks County, Pennsylvania]], and [[Northampton County, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="Clark">{{cite news |last1=Clark |first1=Kathryn Finegan |title=Once upon a time in Durham |url=http://www.buckscountyherald.com/7-12-18/By-the-Way.html |accessdate=16 July 2018 |work=Bucks County Herald |date=2018 |archive-date=16 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180716165940/http://www.buckscountyherald.com/7-12-18/By-the-Way.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Land conservation==
Over a 50 year period, Ned and Linda Heindel have purchased and preserved 128 acres of "forest, bogs and meadows" around the stone farmhouse in which they live, in [[Williams Township, Northampton County, Pennsylvania]]. The hilly area includes stands of ash, poplar and oak trees, wild [[azalea]], freshwater springs and [[Hexenkopf Hill|Hexenkopf Rock]], a ridge of exposed [[Precambrian]] stone.<ref name="Kraus"/>
Linda Heindel serves as the secretary of the Land Preservation Board of Williams Township, Northampton County, PA.<ref name="TWP">{{cite web|title=Land Preservation Board|url=https://www.williamstwp.org/land-preservation/board|website=Williams Township, Northampton County, PA|accessdate=21 February 2018}}</ref>

As of August 2014, a consortium of energy companies  announced plans to build the [[PennEast Pipeline]] to carry [[natural gas]] from the [[Marcellus Shale]] in Pennsylvania into [[New Jersey]]. Ned and Linda Heindel are among residents who would be affected.<ref name="Kraus">{{cite news|last1=Kraus|first1=Scott|last2=Palochko|first2=Jacqueline|title=Proposed 105-mile PennEast pipeline rattles residents|url=http://www.mcall.com/news/local/mc-penneast-pipeline-residents-20141004-story.html|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=The Morning Call|date=October 14, 2014}}</ref>

Beginning on February 6, 2018, the PennEast Pipeline Co. has filed  [[eminent domain]] notices in federal court to take possession of rights of way on the lands of those who have not agreed to the pipeline.<ref name="Hurdle">{{cite news|last1=Hurdle|first1=Jon|title=PennEast pipeline seeks eminent domain, plus U.S. marshals to protect workers|url=https://stateimpact.npr.org/pennsylvania/2018/02/08/penneast-pipeline-seeks-eminent-domain-plus-u-s-marshals-to-protect-workers/|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=StateImpact|agency=NPR|date=February 8, 2018}}</ref> 
Those who received eminent domain notices include at least 129 New Jersey landowners<ref name="Hurdle3">{{cite news|last1=Hurdle|first1=Jon|title=Pipeline Conflict Heats Up: Landowners Vow to Fight PennEast on Eminent Domain|url=http://www.njspotlight.com/stories/18/02/14/pipeline-conflict-heats-up-landowners-vow-to-fight-penneast-on-eminent-domain/|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=NJ Spotlight|date=February 15, 2018}}</ref> and 50 Pennsylvania landowners,<ref name="Hurdle2">{{cite news|last1=Hurdle|first1=Jon|title=Landowners brace for eminent domain loss in PennEast pipeline cases|url=https://stateimpact.npr.org/pennsylvania/2018/02/19/landowners-brace-for-eminent-domain-loss-in-penneast-pipeline-cases/|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=StateImpact|agency=NPR|date=February 19, 2018}}</ref> among them the Heindels.<ref name="Wright">{{cite news|last1=Wright|first1=Emma|title=Residents fight for their land against PennEast pipeline|url=http://www.wfmz.com/news/lehigh-valley/residents-fight-for-their-land-against-penneast-pipeline/704851068|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=69 News|date=February 20, 2018}}</ref>
The Heindels are active opponents of the proposed pipeline and the attempted seizure of their land under eminent domain.<ref name="Palochko">{{cite news|last1=Palochko|first1=Jacqueline|title=Newsmaker Q&A: Linda Heindel, PennEast Pipeline opponent|url=http://www.mcall.com/news/local/mc-newsmaker-linda-heindel-20141108-story.html|accessdate=21 February 2018|work=The Morning Call|date=November 9, 2014}}</ref><ref name="Kraus"/><ref name="Wright"/>

==Death==
Heindel died on June 27, 2023, at the age of 85.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-06 |title=Remembering Emeritus Chemistry Professor Ned D. Heindel |url=https://www2.lehigh.edu/remembering-emeritus-chemistry-professor-ned-d-heindel |access-date=2026-10-11 |website=Lehigh University News |language=en}}</ref>

* 2009, Fellow, [[American Chemical Society]]<ref name="Fellow"/>
* 2002, Ben Franklin Partnership Award for Corporate Assistance<ref name="Berg">{{cite news|last1=Berg|first1=Christian|title=Ben Franklin Technology center honors eight leaders for contribution to economy|url=https://www.mcall.com/2002/05/17/ben-franklin-technology-center-honors-eight-leaders-for-contribution-to-economy-venture-capitalist-guy-kawasaki-delivers-the-keynote-address/|work=The Morning Call|date=May 17, 2002}}</ref> 
* 1997, [[Henry Aaron Hill|Henry Hill]] Award for Achievements in Medicinal Chemistry, [[NOBCChE]]<ref name="NOBCChE">{{cite web|title=Dr. Henry A. Hill Distinguished Lecture|url=http://www.nobcche.org/henry-hill-distinguished-lecture|website=National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref>
* 1996, [[Harry Stone Mosher|Harry and Carol Mosher]] Award for Contributions to Chemistry, ACS<ref>{{cite web|title=Section Awards and Grants|url=http://scvacs.org/?page_id=44|website=American Chemical Society|accessdate=10 October 2017}}</ref>
* 1989, Brady Cancer Achievement Award, Brady Cancer Research Foundation, for research in tumor-imaging radiopharmaceuticals<ref name="Bowker"/><ref name="PDDI"/>
* 1978, Briody Award<ref name="Henderson"/>
* 1969, Robinson Award<ref name="Henderson"/>
